consensus_summary: All three blind responses identify lamp oil primarily as the Holy Spirit — the indwelling presence, anointing, and empowering that sustains the believer's light and cannot be borrowed (Matt 25; Zech 4; Ex 27; 1 Sam 16). Secondary readings include readiness/watchfulness (the modern critical view), good works (Augustinian/patristic), faith or grace (Reformation), and, as a minority/rare view, the Word of God or divine truth as fuel for the lamp.
book_summary: The book defines lamp oil not as the Spirit himself but as Spirit-taught truth and correction that is received, kept (stored in the vessel), and worked into proven obedience — the pressed, tested product of the Spirit's instruction held inwardly; the resulting light is that obedience made visible as an example (Matt 5:16). The book explicitly flags the Holy Spirit/anointing reading as the 'commonly taught' view it is departing from.
rationale: The book's own common-view note acknowledges and then displaces the dominant consensus (oil = Holy Spirit) that all three blind responses name as primary. Its replacement meaning — reproof and truth purchased, stored, and converted into obedient practice — overlaps only partially with minority strands in the consensus (Word/truth as fuel; good works), and adds a distinctive element absent from every blind response: correction/reproof itself as the oil (Ps 141:5, Prov 27:5-6). Because it contradicts the recognizable primary interpretation rather than merely sharpening it, DIVERGENT fits better than REFINED; because fragments of the claim appear in minority alternatives, it is not fully NOVEL.
strongest_objection: Zechariah 4:6 ('not by might... but by my spirit') is printed with the entry and is the classic proof-text that oil symbolizes the Spirit's own power, not merely Spirit-taught instruction; one could argue the book's citations actually reinforce the consensus reading, and that Ps 141:5's 'reproof as excellent oil' concerns anointing oil imagery, not lamp fuel, making the transfer to Matthew 25 an inferential leap rather than direct evidence.
